items.title: Z.ai releases GLM-5.4 featuring its first Loop Transformer to advance generalized coding capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Z.ai has introduced GLM-5.4, a new model incorporating its first Loop Transformer architecture aimed at enhancing generalized coding performance. This development represents a step forward in the company's efforts to improve AI coding models through novel transformer designs. The release has sparked discussion in the developer community, highlighting interest in the potential applications and technical details of the Loop Transformer approach.

items.title: OpenAI argues for using perplexity as a shared metric to track AI model progress and inform safety standards amid emerging capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI's Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki explains that perplexity, a measure of how well AI models predict data, remains a key indicator of AI progress and emerging capabilities. The company advocates for establishing perplexity as a common metric across developers to enhance transparency and safety in AI development. Pachocki details how improvements in perplexity have correlated with significant advances from GPT-2 through GPT-4 and beyond, including breakthroughs in reasoning and specialized fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. OpenAI has begun publishing internal perplexity measurements to foster a shared scientific basis for evaluating AI progress and safety standards industry-wide. The post also highlights the accelerating role of AI in its own development, particularly in algorithmic research on pretraining, which may lead to further rapid advances. OpenAI emphasizes the importance of tracking pretraining progress as a stable and informative measure despite evolving downstream benchmarks and capabilities.

items.title: Guide to setting up local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth on Windows PCs, including hardware requirements and model selection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: This article explains how to run local AI models like Inkling and Qwen on a Windows PC using Unsloth Desktop, enabling private, home-based AI similar to ChatGPT. It covers hardware needs, focusing on GPU VRAM capacity, and how quantized models allow larger AI models to run on consumer-grade graphics cards. The guide provides practical advice on choosing AI models based on VRAM size, with examples ranging from 8GB to 32GB GPUs, and discusses trade-offs involved in quantization. It aims to help beginners set up their own local AI systems without complex software installations or subscriptions, emphasizing privacy and cost savings compared to cloud-based AI services.

items.title: Report: Dario Amodei suggested immersive video games could pacify populations after AI-driven job losses [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Dario Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic, reportedly proposed using immersive video games as a way to address political unrest caused by widespread job displacement due to artificial intelligence. This suggestion was revealed through Slack messages shared internally at Anthropic following the company's IPO. The idea reflects concerns about the societal impact of AI automation and the potential need for unconventional solutions to manage economic and social challenges arising from AI-induced unemployment. The discussion highlights ongoing debates within the AI community about the broader consequences of rapid technological change.

items.title: Developer launches Worker 755, a browser game where players act as subagents to AI managers using real LLMs like Claude and GPT [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Worker 755 is a browser-based game in which players serve as subagents to AI managers powered by large language models such as Claude, GPT, and Gemini. The AI manager assigns tasks with a 90-second timer, and players complete or skip them, receiving performance reviews based on their actions. The game simulates a workplace environment where the AI orchestrates tasks and evaluates player responses in real time. Players can use free shifts on servers with starter credits or bring their own API keys to access various AI models. The game offers options for sandbox or live database environments and supports scripted or AI-driven managers. It runs on Node.js and can be deployed locally or via Docker, with configuration options for API keys and resource limits. The project is open source under the MIT license and includes a detailed design specification and testing framework.

items.title: Comparison of sandboxing tools for AI coding agents including nono, Docker Sandboxes, Microsandbox, and OpenShell highlights trade-offs in security, speed, and usability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: This article evaluates four sandboxing tools-nono, Docker Sandboxes, Microsandbox, and OpenShell-used to isolate AI coding agents and mitigate risks from malicious or unintended actions. It compares their sandboxing methods, credential handling, usability features, and security limitations, noting that none have reached full maturity and all have strengths and weaknesses. The analysis emphasizes the importance of sandboxing due to widespread AI coding agent use and vulnerabilities like prompt injection, which can manipulate agent behavior. It also discusses real-world incidents illustrating the consequences of inadequate sandboxing and highlights gaps common to all tools, such as limited syscall customization and lack of integrated management interfaces. The article concludes that while sandboxing reduces risk, it is not foolproof, and proper configuration remains critical to limit potential damage from compromised AI agents or hallucinations.

items.title: Customer sues bank after AI agent rejects loan application, raising questions about accountability and transparency in AI decisions [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A customer is suing a bank following the rejection of their loan application by an AI agent, highlighting challenges in understanding and proving the reasons behind AI-driven decisions in financial services. The case underscores concerns about accountability and transparency when automated systems make critical determinations affecting individuals. This legal action may prompt closer scrutiny of AI decision-making processes and the need for clearer explanations in automated financial approvals.

items.title: Researchers say AI may have solved the Riemann Hypothesis, raising questions about human comprehension of the proof
items.content_text: An AI system has reportedly found a solution to the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems. The discovery marks a significant milestone in AI-assisted mathematical research but presents challenges for human mathematicians in understanding and verifying the AI-generated proof. Experts are now examining the implications of relying on AI for complex mathematical discoveries and the potential need for new methods to interpret such proofs.

items.title: METR report finds AI models improve coding but struggle with judgment tasks; research raises concerns about crop yield impact from enhanced rock weathering carbon removal [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR reveals that while AI capabilities in coding are advancing rapidly, models face significant challenges with tasks requiring judgment, such as designing evaluations and scoring philosophical arguments. This highlights limitations in AI's ability to automate complex research and development functions. Meanwhile, research into enhanced rock weathering-a carbon removal method involving spreading crushed rock on farmland-indicates that adding too much material could reduce crop yields, suggesting the approach's carbon capture potential may be smaller than previously thought. These findings underscore ongoing challenges in both AI development and environmental sustainability efforts.

items.title: Lianex launches unified search tool for eBay, Amazon Australia, JB Hi-Fi, and other retailers
items.content_text: Lianex has introduced a search platform that enables users to query multiple online retailers including eBay, Amazon Australia, and JB Hi-Fi simultaneously. The tool aggregates product listings from these platforms into a single interface to streamline the shopping experience.

items.title: SwiftTerm maintainer reflects on evolving AI-driven contributions to open-source, noting shifts from flawed fixes to more accurate pull requests over seven years [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The maintainer of SwiftTerm, an open-source terminal emulator library, shares insights from seven years of managing contributions, highlighting how AI involvement in pull requests has grown from early flawed attempts to more reliable fixes. Initially, many AI-generated patches were superficial or incorrect, but recent contributions increasingly address real user issues effectively. The article discusses challenges such as contributors relying on AI without deep understanding of the codebase and the emergence of "Promptsplainers" who overestimate AI-generated solutions. Despite these hurdles, the maintainer values AI-assisted pull requests as they provide concrete starting points for resolving real-world problems, marking a significant change in open-source collaboration dynamics.

items.title: Leopold Aschenbrenner continues heavy AI investments despite record losses at Situational Awareness hedge fund [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Leopold Aschenbrenner, manager of the San Francisco-based hedge fund Situational Awareness LP, has maintained his commitment to artificial intelligence investments despite suffering one of the largest trading losses in American stock-market history this summer. The fund lost about two-thirds of its value after previously achieving returns over 1,000% from late 2024 to mid-2026, mostly through AI industry investments. Aschenbrenner believes the AI revolution is accelerating rapidly and predicts 2027 will see AI growth two to five times faster than before, with AI infrastructure spending rivaling the U.S. defense budget. He has held a significant stake in Anthropic, an AI company recently valued at about $1.5 trillion, which he considers the fund's most prized asset despite the recent losses. Aschenbrenner expects AI to automate AI research itself, potentially leading to superintelligence, though this has not yet occurred.

This admission highlights the challenges faced by officials in adapting to new forms of academic dishonesty enabled by emerging technologies.

items.title: Independent mathematicians confirm AI-generated proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct after verification using Lean programming language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have verified that the AI-generated proof of the Riemann hypothesis, produced using Anthropic's Claude model by mathematician Levent Alpöge, is valid. Independent mathematicians compiled and checked the proof using the Lean mathematics programming language, confirming its correctness without errors or shortcuts. The verification process included ensuring the proof addressed the actual Riemann hypothesis and did not alter any mathematical definitions or rules. A final comparator run confirmed the proof's integrity, leading the Lean and Mathlib communities to officially certify the statement and proof as correct.

items.title: Researchers say enhanced rock weathering for carbon removal may reduce crop yields, limiting its climate impact to under one billion tons of CO2 annually
items.content_text: Tech companies including Google and Microsoft have invested heavily in enhanced rock weathering (ERW), spreading crushed alkaline rocks on farms to capture carbon dioxide and improve soil quality. However, new preprint studies led by CarbonPlan researchers suggest that applying too much rock could harm crop yields, which would constrain the method's carbon removal potential to less than one billion tons per year. This raises concerns about the scalability and effectiveness of ERW as a climate solution. Enhanced rock weathering accelerates natural processes by increasing rock surface area to react with atmospheric CO2, potentially locking carbon in ocean sediments over time. While ERW can improve soil nutrients and acidity, benefiting some farmers, the new findings highlight a trade-off between soil amendment benefits and crop productivity. These results add to ongoing scientific debates about accurately measuring ERW's carbon removal and its practical limits in agriculture.

items.title: Report: Frontier AI companies increasingly delegate AI R&D decision-making to internal AI agents, raising Loss of Control risks and national security concerns [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.content_text: A new research report highlights that leading frontier AI companies are progressively handing off AI research and development functions, including high-level decisions, to internally deployed AI agents. This shift, termed 'Handoff,' accelerates AI capabilities but increases risks of misalignment and loss of human oversight, potentially leading to uncontrollable AI behavior. The report warns that this trend is advancing rapidly, with some companies already having AI agents write the majority of their code and conduct reviews, and calls for policymakers to gain visibility and implement governance measures to mitigate these risks.

items.title: Apex verify launches an independent AI model to write and run missing tests on AI-generated code changes, improving detection of errors missed by original tests [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Apex verify is a tool that uses a separate AI model to generate additional tests for code changes made by AI coding agents, aiming to catch errors that pass the original tests but do not meet the task requirements. It runs these new checks alongside existing tests on a copy of the code, providing a verdict of ready, not ready, or unknown with evidence, without modifying the original project. The tool integrates with various development workflows, including GitHub pull requests and Claude Code sessions, and supports multiple testing frameworks. In evaluations on 200 AI-generated code changes, Apex verify identified about 80% of incorrect changes that passed original tests, though it still misses some errors and occasionally flags correct changes. It is designed to enhance confidence in AI-assisted coding by independently verifying that code changes fulfill their intended tasks.

items.title: Hashimoto launches Rex, a free terminal emulator and multiplexer with persistent sessions and remote connections, beginning public testing on macOS
items.content_text: Hashimoto has started public testing of Rex, a new terminal emulator and multiplexer designed to replace existing terminals with improved user experience, persistent sessions, and performant remote connections. Initially available on macOS, Rex can self-host its own server and connect across devices, with plans to expand support to Linux, Windows, and iOS clients. The product has undergone private testing with about 50 users and is reported to be stable, though public testing aims to identify and fix edge cases. Rex is free, requires no account, supports full self-hosting, and does not share user data. Invitations to the test program are being sent in waves, with a stable public release planned after the testing phase.

The event will feature WIRED editors and correspondents who will answer audience questions about AI safety and Big Tech's role in addressing these challenges.

items.title: Asus launches ProArt P16 laptop with Nvidia RTX Spark chip and up to 128GB RAM to run large local AI models, priced up to $7,000 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Asus has introduced the ProArt P16 laptop featuring Nvidia's new RTX Spark chip and up to 128GB of LPDDR5x RAM, enabling it to run large AI models locally without relying on cloud services. The device combines AI capabilities with gaming and productivity functions, running Windows 11 to support local AI agents more easily. The laptop includes a 16-inch 4K+ OLED display, multiple USB-C ports, and a high-capacity battery, though its top-end model costs up to $7,000. Nvidia and Asus position the ProArt P16 as a powerful workstation capable of handling frontier-level AI workloads on a portable device.

items.title: Zhou Yu discusses using dynamic simulations to evaluate conversational AI agents, addressing non-deterministic LLM behavior and testing across personas, goals, and corner cases [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Zhou Yu, a computer science professor and AI expert, explains how dynamic simulations can effectively evaluate conversational AI agents whose actions depend on prior responses and non-deterministic language models. She emphasizes that static benchmarks are insufficient and that simulations incorporating diverse personas, goals, and environmental factors provide more accurate testing. Simulations can be applied throughout the software lifecycle, aiding product design, continuous integration testing, stress testing before deployment, and monitoring production for model drift or third-party tool failures. They also support compliance verification across regions and enable fine-tuning with synthetic data. Detailed logging during simulations offers audit trails for regulatory compliance and failure analysis.

items.title: 22radar.com publishes public audit of AI agent's autonomous work signing and error tracking, revealing gaps in content verification controls [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: 22radar.com conducted a public audit of its AI assistant, Claude by Anthropic, which autonomously signed its own work but produced errors that were openly documented to enhance transparency. The audit revealed that while controls over the AI's actions and publishing approvals were effective, there were significant shortcomings in verifying the truthfulness of the AI-generated content, including missing validity indicators and independent checks. The audit detailed a timeline of 39 error instances linked to repeated causes, showing that corrections were made individually without systemic error detection. The site's crypto rankings were anchored on a blockchain test network with dual signatures from the AI and the owner, but automatic publishing was halted due to GitHub restrictions, requiring manual updates. The findings highlight the challenges in AI governance, particularly in ensuring content accuracy and maintaining a single source of truth across deliverables.

items.title: Telnyx launches AI Assistants for WhatsApp messaging with unified number handling voice, SMS, and WhatsApp channels [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Telnyx has introduced AI Assistants that can now manage WhatsApp messaging conversations alongside voice calls using the same assistant logic and knowledge base. This integration allows businesses to use a single Telnyx number for PSTN voice, SMS, WhatsApp messaging, and calling, simplifying management and analytics. The new feature supports both template and free-form messaging within WhatsApp's 24-hour customer conversation window and uses webhook-based message handling to trigger AI responses. This enables real-time customer support, appointment reminders, order updates, and multi-language support without requiring separate bots or platforms for WhatsApp and voice channels.

items.title: Sashiko AI adds Linux Performance Specialist review stage to linux_patch_review with benchmarking and false-positive tracking [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Sashiko AI has introduced an optional Linux Performance Specialist review stage to its linux_patch_review tool, aiming to improve detection of performance regressions in kernel patches. This stage integrates specialized analysis with benchmarking and false-positive tracking to enhance evaluation accuracy for non-trivial code changes in C, Rust, or struct/header files. The new review stage includes second-order side-effect tracing, anti-noise guardrails, and a balanced benchmark suite of 40 commits combining upstream regressions and clean commits. Testing showed a significant increase in positive detection rates with minimal false positives and moderate resource overhead, supporting more reliable performance assessments during patch reviews.

items.title: Local AI Tool Engine moves planning into code to improve reliability of small local LLM agents for multi-step tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Local AI Tool Engine (L.A.T.E.) is a new framework that enhances the reliability of small local large language models (LLMs) by shifting the planning logic from the model into plain code. This approach enables the model to focus on generating text while exact computations, file operations, and multi-step workflows are handled by dedicated tools and code, improving accuracy and consistency even with smaller models. L.A.T.E. supports tasks like web search, file reading and writing, math calculations, and memory across chats, running locally with models from Ollama, LM Studio, or OpenAI-compatible APIs without requiring paid services or complex dependencies. The system executes jobs step-by-step, reports exact outcomes, and avoids hallucinations by relying on real tools for factual operations. It offers both terminal and browser interfaces and automatically manages dependencies and model selection.

items.title: Physicist analyzes feasibility and challenges of deploying AI data centers in space [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A physicist critically examines the concept of placing AI data centers in space, highlighting the practical difficulties and technical constraints involved. The analysis addresses the physical and engineering challenges that make such projects complex and questions their overall viability. This perspective provides a grounded assessment of the idea beyond speculative enthusiasm.

items.title: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produces machine-verifiable proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem using novel strategy in Lean, leading Autoform-Hard benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra independently generated a formal, machine-verifiable proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem using the Lean proof assistant, marking the first known proof of this 2006 theorem in Lean. The model developed its own proof strategy due to missing foundational elements in the Mathlib library, employing a metric called "capacity" to measure growth in mathematical systems. This achievement occurred on the Autoform-Hard benchmark, a challenging subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench with 56 tasks that previous models failed to solve within budget. Astra completed the proof after nearly 94 minutes and $21.58 in compute costs, surpassing other models by solving 49 tasks, and currently leads the leaderboard ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2.

items.title: Gostudio.ai launches AI photo and video studio with 38 one-click editing tools and 20+ handpicked AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Gostudio.ai offers an AI-powered photo and video studio featuring 38 one-click tools for tasks like relighting, background swapping, and aging photos. The platform supports personal branding with AI-generated headshots, hairstyle changes, and video creation from still images, all accessible without subscriptions through a credit-based system. Users can edit photos and videos using specialized AI models tailored for each task, including cultural and identity-preserving edits, product integration, and cinematic effects. Gostudio.ai provides flexible pricing plans with no credit card required for initial free credits, aiming to simplify and consolidate AI-driven media editing in one platform.

items.title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI-generated music from Repentance Plus after discovery and Steam review backlash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]

The AI music was found in a Grand Theft Auto-themed segment, with files traced to Suno's generative AI platform. McMillen apologized on social media, stating he was unaware of the AI music's inclusion, and the studio Nicalis did not disclose its use as required by Valve's policies. Despite the removal, the game continues to receive overwhelmingly negative reviews on Steam, though some users have expressed support for McMillen's stance against AI in game development.

items.title: Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford invested billions in Anthropic before its record $81.3 billion IPO, citing strong developer adoption and consistent execution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford made significant investments in AI startup Anthropic prior to its November 2026 IPO, which raised $81.3 billion and valued the company at about $1.5 trillion. These investors were convinced by Anthropic's growing developer preference for its Claude model, rising enterprise adoption, and consistent business execution despite high valuations and competition from rivals like OpenAI. Notable Capital allocated roughly 10% of its U.S. fund to Anthropic's Series E, noting a shift in developer usage favoring Claude over ChatGPT. GIC began investing after seeing early signs of enterprise traction with Claude Code and led later funding rounds, investing over $4.5 billion for about a 1% stake post-IPO. Baillie Gifford committed $1.5 billion across three rounds, impressed by Anthropic's expansion into legal, life sciences, and cybersecurity sectors and its strong financial performance. These investments reflect confidence in U.S.-based closed-source AI models amid geopolitical complexities and the belief that developers are key early adopters driving AI growth. The paper returns from these bets have been substantial, marking one of the largest venture-scale windfalls in recent years.

items.title: Can Jensen Really Return?
items.content_text: Welcome, Weekenders! Jensen Huang wants a mulligan, and a good number of people seem keen to let him have one. On Tuesday, just days after the longtime Nvidia CEO resigned the job, Huang said in a statement he'd be open to taking back the job. Depending on your perspective, that suggestion is akin to letting a skunked dog back into bed-or a veritable Second Coming. For now, Nvidia's board is holding firm and has continued to insist it won't rehire Huang. One of the most prominent calls for Huang's return came on Friday, with President Donald Trump saying he thought Nvidia should give Huang his job back. "We're a country of second chances," Trump said. "He's a man ... who made some bad decisions." (Surely a situation Trump himself could understand.) In addition to Trump, a good number of industry pooh-bahs have continued to voice support for their fallen comrade and advocating for Huang was definitely a major topic on this week's very busy conference circuit. That support came in both implicit and explicit terms. At the New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk was blunt, saying "there's no one who can really replace" Huang. At the TomorrowX conference, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Musk groupie Antonio Gracias donned black leather jackets to show their solidarity. And during a Semafor shindig in San Francisco, Sam Altman described Huang as a personal hero, Jeff Bezos said he was a "remarkable guy" and investor Bill Ackman labeled him as "one of the most iconic CEOs of all time." On X, Ackman has been theorizing about how Huang could actually return. Ackman (and venture capitalist Garry Tan) has been trumpeting a roundabout plan that involves getting together a 15% ownership block of Nvidia to call a special shareholder meeting and then ... vote out the anti-Huang board members ... and swing the board to a pro-Huang majority? It's somewhat unclear. (Apparently, Huang still has some allies on the board; remember, we told you that the board hadn't initially wanted to act at all.) "Ackman's idea is somewhere between extremely unlikely and remote," said Jeffrey Gordon, a Columbia University law professor and former Treasury Department attorney. (Or, in other words, as likely as defrosting a 20-pound Thanksgiving turkey overnight.) The proposal does seem to assume Huang supporters could really rile up Wall Street institutions with major Nvidia stakes, such as BlackRock, and get them to go activist-not a certain thing at all. It also conveniently ignores how difficult the math for a board-ousting vote looks when factoring in how much institutional money is held in passive-investing funds, which will never throw support behind an insurrection. Rather than a board coup, Huang's clearest route to returning would be if the board caves and changes its mind. Sure, it might, eventually. But we have to get through the many, many inquiries into Huang and Nvidia that have popped up and who knows what else we'll learn in the meantime, especially since there are a lotttt of people newly determined to peer into every Nvidia crevice: journalists galore, the SEC, the Commerce and Justice Departments, a trio of Congressional committees and possibly the FBI. The Huang situation keeps getting likened to Altman's ouster from OpenAI in 2023, which obviously ended with Altman's return. I don't think the comparison holds up. Most obviously, OpenAI was a private company-its board had more freedom to change its mind. And as Gordon pointed out to me, Altman's reinstatement came after a true mass rebellion of OpenAI staff: roughly 745 out of 770 employees signed a letter threatening to go with Altman to Microsoft, more than 95% of the company. Now, a letter supporting Huang's reinstatement is floating around the internet, and it purports to have signatures from 10,263 Nvidia employees. Even if they were all legit signatures, they represent only a quarter of the company's workforce. Maybe most Nvidians, as they call themselves, actually didn't like Huang's rampant humiliation tactics, which reportedly once included a threat to scalp someone and piss on their brain. Maybe most of them are comfortable living without him. I mean, sure, I'd totally get why!-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Nvidia Introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang for Workaround on U.S. Export Controls Jensen Huang's Right-Hand Man Oversaw Chip Customers-Including Alice Huang To Strengthen OpenAI, Brockman Goes 'Full Management Mode' 'Theranos But Real': New Blood-Testing Startup Says It Can Predict Health Risks Listening: "Stories of Art" After weeks like the ones we've just had, I like to make it a point to visit a museum and spend some time staring at ancient, beautiful things-a chance to relish the creative ingenuity of humans who never once heard the phrase "forward-deployed engineer." Truthfully, though, the tech action has lately been so fast-paced that I still haven't gotten to make one of those pilgrimages, so I've been counterprogramming my brain with a binge through "Stories of Art," a podcast about, yes, art-from Renaissance Florence to Basquiat's lower Manhattan loft-that launched earlier in the year. (Apple recently declared it one of 2026's best.) The hosts are a pair of amiable Brits, art historian James Fox and art critic Alastair Sooke, who take a cheerful, conversational approach to what might otherwise be dry recountings. In effect, they are to Renoir what "The Rest Is History" lads are to the Romans. (Given the subject matter of "Stories of Art"-namely, art-I suggest you watch the podcast's video version when you can. While Fox and Sooke are quite adept at describing the artworks they mention, it's nice to actually see what they're talking about.) Nearly all the artists who get mentioned achieved their fame through real entrepreneurial verve, challenging the entrenched status quo. (Sounds like a familiar motivation, right?) Take Claude Monet and the birth of Impressionism: The movement traces its origins to a decision in 1874 by Monet and a group of other artists to refuse to exhibit their work at an established gallery. Instead, they formed their own company (yes, founder mode Monet!) and then set up their own Paris exhibition space that featured newfangled technology, such as elevators. Many of you will enjoy one of the most recent episodes on James Whistler, a fellow who took a real dim view of journalists and pursued a high-profile libel lawsuit against one critic. A warning about how that turned out for Whistler: He did triumph in court. He then promptly went bankrupt.-Abram Brown Reading: "Fruit Fly" by Josh Silver In suburban north London, author Mallory Maddox seems to have a rich, full life: a handsome Netflix-executive husband, a townhome with $2,000 armchairs and dusky-pink walls and a literary world standing as a "modern-day Virginia Woolf," as one reviewer has christened her. Yet appearances are almost always deceiving in "Fruit Fly," a spry, tart satire of sex and 21st century storytelling: Mallory's relationship with hubbie Ronan has turned stiff and chilly, and as much as he thinks about the bedroom, it's to insist that it's time for kids. ("I haven't had an orgasm in years," she recalls in an ongoing inner monologue.) Professionally, Mallory is dogged by "a shadowy, persisting darkness"-a profound case of writer's block. To fill the time, she moonlights as an online therapist and hunts exhaustively for those expensive home furnishings. Desperate for writerly inspiration, she peruses Reddit-uh oh-and takes to heart another author's comment about the state of the publishing industry: "go dark, go gay." She downloads Grindr, sets up an account with a few of her husband's nudes and scores an invite to an orgy at a house down the street. She never actually sets foot inside but nevertheless makes the acquaintance of Leo, an attractive but homeless and drug-addicted gay man who sells himself to other men. (As the novel shifts perspectives, Leo contributes his own inner thoughts, which are often mordant and felonious. "Old women carry cash. Everyone knows that," he thinks, snatching a purse. "Someone should tell them to stop.") Mallory offers to counsel Leo-pro bono, bless her-and begins writing a novel that lightly fictionalizes his frayed life. For a time, he believes she's just a daffy do-gooder. ("This is weird," Leo thinks as she leads him through a silent-breathing exercise. "This is very fucking weird, but I guess I've done weirder things.") And her publishers absolutely adore what she is finally putting on the page. As one editor remarks: "It's so bleak-but also somehow so funny?" Much the same can be said about "Fruit Fly" itself.-A.B. Watching: "The Weight" President Franklin Roosevelt attempted to govern Depression-era America through no small number of novel schemes: A good many of them are quite famous, such as Social Security. A few have disappeared into history, including Roosevelt's 1933 executive order that banned gold hoarding, forcing Americans to turn over large stockpiles of the precious metal. (No one could keep more than $100 worth.) That presidential decision is the inciting force in "The Weight," a tense wilderness thriller starring Ethan Hawke as Murphy, leader of a group of convicts hired by their jailer (Russell Crowe) to heist a gold mine's reserves. It's part of a plan that's complex in the same way that "Goldfinger" is not actually a film about robbing Fort Knox. Often, heist films are fabulous capers, with champagne, tuxedos and bon mots. "The Weight" very much is not, depicting a bloodied-knuckled trek across the Oregon backwoods, with Murphy and his thieves weighed down, literally, by their bullion-filled backpacks and, metaphorically, by their past misdeeds and inner demons. Still, Murphy is well incentivized to make it through. In a true miscarriage of justice, he has been separated from his plucky daughter, Penny (Avy Berry); part of his reward for orchestrating the robbery is early release, which will let him reclaim her. "The Weight" does take a moment to get going. Then it really rips, with a pair of memorable fight scenes that are a real credit to both the film's editing and cinematography.-A.B.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO Triumph [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic pulled it off. The biggest pure-play AI company out there, maker of the Claude line of AI models, went public on Thursday, with its shares jumping as much as 39% above its IPO price. The stock settled back a bit to close at $97.17, up 17% from its IPO price. That gave it a market capitalization of $1.76 trillion, assuming you include all options, restricted stock units and convertible notes that might one day become shares. Not bad for a company that's just five years old. What makes the IPO even more notable is that it occurred despite months of investor jitters about the cost of AI development. Partly as a result of those jitters, we've had a very choppy market that has stalled IPO plans by a slew of other companies-including data center developers SB Energy and Nscale that filed publicly over the summer. Notably, SB Energy on Thursday updated its IPO filing for the first time since late September, suggesting it was still hoping to go public, while Nscale updated its filing a week ago also for the first time since September. But Anthropic's success doesn't mean the IPO market has opened up. "I don't think this opens the floodgates unless you look like Anthropic," Lise Buyer, managing partner of Class V Group, said on a subscriber video discussion convened by The Information.

items.title: Why Anthropic's VC Investors Aren't Letting Go [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Earlier this week I reported that at least four venture firms were in line to make at least 10 times their investment in Anthropic, whose shares closed up 17% on the first day of trading Thursday. For many venture capitalists and the endowments and foundations that invest in VC funds, the offering is the first step to turning private shares into cash. But some VCs want even more of the company: Sequoia Capital and Iconiq had planned to buy more shares at the IPO, a person familiar with the firms' thinking said. Lightspeed Venture Partners and Accel intended to do the same, Bloomberg News reported Tuesday. And Altimeter CEO Brad Gerstner told CNBC his firm aimed to invest $5 billion in the IPO. Many of these investors already stand to reap billions from Anthropic's IPO: Iconiq and Lightspeed hold some of the largest VC stakes, valued at over $27 billion each based on the size of their stakes before the IPO.
